# Introduction

Being a researcher is a profession that not many can occupy. For it to
work in a society, researchers compete over actual and artificially
limited resources such as number of jobs and grant money but also
publications in prestigious journals. While the assessment of the
quality of research, institutions, and researchers is a substantial part
of the system, the assessment is not rewarded. Instead, research quality
assessment often uses shortcuts such as the number and type of
publications, the prestige of the country that they are living in, the
prestige of the institution that they work at, or the number of
citations of their research or the journals that they published their
research in. The most prominent assessment tool is the Journal Impact Factor (JIF). The JIF of an academic journal is a
proprietary value owned by the data analytics business Clarivate and
based on their literature database "Web of Science". It is not openly
available but has to be purchased (the costs for a university to access
the Web of Science are around EUR 100,000 per year), and most
importantly, its computation violates basic statistical assumptions
(since it is the arithmetic mean for a heavily skewed distribution) and
it not suited as a proxy for quality [@Simons2008]. Past studies could
show that, if anything, it is negatively related to objective criteria
of quality [@Brembs2018] and even its inventor has lamented its frequent
misuse [@Hecht1998]. In recent years, researchers have been trying to
shift research assessment away from citation metrics and more heavily
rely on qualitative criteria of research items. For example, as of March
19, 2026, 26,997 individuals and organizations have signed the San
Francisco Declaration on Research Assessment, which is the commitment to
not only rely on the Journal Impact Factor [@american2012san].

At the same time, scrutiny of research quality is rising with higher
transparency requirements (e.g., code and data sharing). While
replication had been at the core of many areas of research [@King1995],
it was only after the majority of 100 replications in psychology failed
[@osc2015] that the number of replications has increased drastically and
journals have become more eager to accept them across numerous
disciplines [e.g., @nosek2013call]. While replication success and
failure is not an indicator of research quality [e.g., @handbook], it is
relevant when researchers build on past findings and since a high number
of citations is predictive of the future number of citations and thus
how many researchers may build on a published findings, the question
arises how citation metrics and replicability are related and how
researchers believe them to be related. Note that with replicability, we
mean the repeated testing of a previously published claim with
*different data*. We refer to repeated tests with *the same data* as
reproductions. Only some of our arguments also work for reproductions and they should be revisited once there is a more comprehensive database of reproduction attempts.

## Should Replicability Indicate Research Quality? (Normative View)

A replication does not necessarily corroborate an original study's
quality. @handbook discuss a phenomenon-focused and a theory-focused
view: The former suggests that a failed replication could merely
indicate limits of generalizability while the latter could disconfirm an
entire theory. A successful replication, on the other hand, would expand
a phenomenon's generalizability but not inform a theory since its
generalizability to new contexts had already been assumed. Moreover,
replication failures can be due to lack of clarity in the original
article or lack of resources in the replication. In summary, we do not
think that replicability should be a measure of research quality. When
comparing fields, some involve more tacit knowledge than others so that
different rates of replicability would be observed that do not inform
quality. Moreover, it is uncertain how stable and heterogeneous phenomena
of interest are across research disciplines. For example, "laws of
nature" may be more static than regularities in animal and human
behavior, indicating that perfect replicability might even be an
unrealistic goal.

## Does Replicability Track Research Quality Empirically? (Descriptive View)

So far, there have been no systematic tests that correlate research
quality and replicability. Researchers could predict replication
outcomes in prediction markets [e.g., @Forsell2019] so one could expect
that reviewers might reject articles that they believe to be
non-replicable and high quality journals would have a relatively high
proportion of replicable findings. At the same time, academic journals
have been encouraged to publish research that they expect to get cited
much. The citation culture in several areas is to provide supportive
(often selective) evidence and with contradictory results in many areas
[e.g., @Friese2018] and cases of citation of a null finding as
supportive [e.g., @Hussey2026], we do not expect researchers to assess
the replicability before choosing to cite an article. This is why have investigated the relationship between replicability and a journal-level citation metric.

Note that while the Clarivate Journal Impact Factor is the most widely
known citation metric, it is proprietary and not openly accessible.
For the present study, we therefore operationalized journal-level
citation impact using the 2-year mean citedness provided by OpenAlex
[@priem2022openalexfullyopenindexscholarly], an open bibliometric
index. This metric is conceptually analogous to the Journal Impact
Factor (i.e., the average number of citations received by articles
published in a journal over the preceding two years) but is computed
from the openly available database OpenAlex (OMC). We refered to this metric as the journal's
impact factor in our study and  refer to it as OMC in this report. Due to the high correlation between different citation metrics, we expect our findings to be generalizable to journal-level citation metrics.

**Replicability Hypothesis**: Journal-level citation metrics are unrelated to replicability of the studies published in the respective journals.

## Is Replicability *being used as* a Measure of Research Quality?

Since misuse of citation metrics is a well-documented phenomenon, we
believe that this extends to the assessment of replicability. In our
study, we explored how strongly this is the case for different
groups of researchers and non-researchers. We tested how strongly this is the case for different groups of participants, including researchers at various career stages and non-researchers.

**General Prediction Hypothesis**: Participants rely on journal-level citation impact
to predict replicability, and this reliance varies by career stage and
educational background.

**Prediction Hypothesis 1:** When the OMC is visible, participants will 
be more likely to predict "success" for studies published in 
higher-OMC journals (positive coefficient for the 
if_visible × impact_factor_z interaction).

**Prediction Hypothesis 2:** This reliance on OMC will be stronger among 
participants with research experience than among those without 
(positive coefficient for the in_research × if_visible × impact_factor_z 
three-way interaction).

Beyond testing these hypotheses, a secondary aim of the present study
was to create a pedagogical tool that raises awareness of replication
research and the difficulty to infer replication results based on original studies. The game was designed to be used in teaching [e.g., via CC0-licensed teaching slides, @roseler2026gutherslides], exposing players to the concept of
replicability and to the diversity of replication outcomes across
disciplines.
